title: Components & Props
summary: **Components** are reusable, self-contained pieces of UI written as functions, and **props** are the read-only inputs a parent passes down to configure them.

subtopics.title: Function components
subtopics.explanation: A function component is just a JavaScript function that accepts a single props object and returns JSX describing a piece of UI. They matter because they are the modern standard for writing React (replacing most class components) and pair naturally with Hooks for state and effects. The key rules: the function name must be capitalized so JSX treats it as a component, and it must return a single root element (or a Fragment).

subtopics.title: Props
subtopics.explanation: Props are the read-only inputs a parent passes down to configure a child component, supplied as a single object of named values. They matter because they are how data flows through a React app — every component is configured by the props its parent gives it. The critical gotcha is that props are immutable inside the child: a component must never reassign or mutate its props; to change them, the parent re-renders with new values.

subtopics.title: Composition
subtopics.explanation: Composition is the practice of building complex UI by nesting smaller, reusable components together, rather than duplicating markup or building deep inheritance hierarchies. It matters because it is React's core reuse mechanism — favoring composition over duplication keeps components small and single-responsibility. You compose by rendering components inside other components and by passing content through the children prop.

subtopics.title: Children prop
subtopics.explanation: Whatever JSX you nest between a component's opening and closing tags is passed to it automatically as the special children prop. This matters because it lets you build flexible wrapper/container components (Card, Modal, Panel) that don't need to know what content they hold. The component simply renders {children} wherever the nested content should appear.

subtopics.title: Destructuring props
subtopics.explanation: Instead of reading props.name and props.role, you destructure the props object directly in the function's parameter list. This matters for readability — it makes a component's expected inputs visible at a glance and removes repetitive props. prefixes throughout the body. It is purely a JavaScript convenience and is the conventional style in modern React.

subtopics.title: Default props
subtopics.explanation: Default prop values let a component fall back to a sensible value when a prop is omitted, written as a default in the destructuring assignment. This matters because it makes props optional and keeps callers concise. It also fixes a common beginner mistake — supplying a fallback by reassigning the prop (which mutates it) instead of declaring a default, which is the correct, immutable approach.

subtopics.title: Props vs state
subtopics.explanation: Props are inputs passed in from a parent and are immutable inside the child; state is internal data a component owns and can change over time. This distinction is the single most common React fundamentals question. The rule of thumb: if a value comes from outside and the component shouldn't change it, it's props; if the component manages and updates it, it's state. Data flows down via props, and updates flow up via callback props.

subtopics.title: Prop drilling
subtopics.explanation: Prop drilling is threading a prop down through several intermediate components that don't use it themselves, just to reach a distant descendant. It matters because it makes code verbose and fragile as trees get deep. It happens naturally from React's one-way data flow; common fixes are composition (passing JSX via children so intermediates never see the data) or React Context for genuinely cross-cutting values — but one or two levels of explicit props is often clearer than over-engineering.

foundations.overview: A React component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX describing a piece of UI. Props are the arguments passed into that function — a single object of named values the parent supplies. Components let you split the UI into independent, reusable pieces, and props let you configure each piece without rewriting it.
foundations.formalDefinition:
A function component is a function that accepts a single `props` object and returns a React element (JSX). Props are immutable inputs owned by the parent: `function Greeting(props) { return

Hello, {props.name}

; }`, used as ``. Data flows in one direction — from parent to child.
foundations.whyItMatters: Components and props are the entire foundation of React. Every React app is a tree of components configured by props. Understanding how data flows down through props — and that props are read-only — is the prerequisite for understanding state, rendering, and every other React concept.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a component as a function that turns data into UI, and props as the arguments to that function. Just as you'd call formatPrice(9.99), you 'call' a component with <PriceTag amount={9.99} />. The parent decides the arguments; the child just renders them.
foundations.browserPerspective: Components don't exist in the DOM. React calls your component functions, collects the returned elements into a tree (the virtual DOM), and then translates that tree into real DOM nodes. The browser only ever sees the final HTML elements — <div>, <h1>, <button> — never your Greeting or Card components.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Buttons, cards, navigation bars, avatars, form fields, modals, list items — every visible part of a UI is a component. Props configure them: a Button takes a label and onClick, an Avatar takes a src and size, a Card takes a title and children.
foundations.businessImpact: Reusable components mean features ship faster and look consistent. A well-designed component library lets a team build new pages by composing existing pieces instead of rewriting markup, which directly cuts development time and reduces visual bugs that erode user trust.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Composition over duplication is the core engineering value. Small, focused components with clear props are easy to test, reason about, and reuse. Misusing props (mutating them, drilling them through many layers) is a common source of fragile, hard-to-maintain code.
foundations.performanceImpact: Components are cheap to define but each one React renders has a cost. Passing new object/array/function props on every render can defeat memoization and cause children to re-render unnecessarily. Keeping props stable and component trees shallow keeps rendering fast.
commonUseCases: Reusable UI primitives (Button, Input, Card, Badge)
Layout containers that wrap arbitrary children (Modal, Panel, Section)
List items rendered from data via .map() with props per item
Presentational components configured entirely by props from a parent

commonMisconceptions.myth: A child component can change its own props to update itself.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Props are read-only. A child must never mutate props. To change what a child shows, the parent re-renders with new prop values, or you lift the value into state owned by the parent.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Props and state are basically the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Props are inputs passed in from a parent and are immutable inside the child. State is data the component owns and can change. Data flows down via props; updates flow up via callbacks.

visualExplorer.title: Data flows down the component tree
visualExplorer.caption: Each box is a component; arrows are props passed from parent to child. Notice data only ever moves downward — this one-way flow is what makes React predictable.

interactiveExamples.title: A component that takes a prop
interactiveExamples.explanation: Greeting receives a name prop from App and renders it. The parent decides the value; the child just displays it. Reuse the same component with different props.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Three headings: Hello, Ada! / Hello, Linus! / Hello, Grace!

interactiveExamples.title: Composition with the children prop
interactiveExamples.explanation: A Card component wraps whatever JSX you nest inside it via the special children prop. This is composition — building complex UI by nesting reusable containers.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Two bordered cards; the content nested inside each <Card> tag appears below its title.

codeLab.title: Build a reusable UserBadge
codeLab.instructions: Create a UserBadge component that takes name and role props and renders 'name — role'. Give role a default value of 'Member' using destructuring defaults, then render two badges from App: one with a role and one without.
hints: Destructure props in the parameter list: function UserBadge({ name, role }) { ... }
Add a default in the destructure: { name, role = 'Member' } — used only when the prop is omitted.

debuggingLab.title: Trying to mutate a prop
debuggingLab.symptom: The component tries to 'reset' its title by assigning to the prop, but the change doesn't stick and React behaves unpredictably.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Props are read-only inputs owned by the parent. Reassigning the destructured variable here happens to compile, but it expresses the wrong mental model: a child must never treat props as mutable. The correct way to supply a fallback is a default value or derived value, not reassignment.
commonMistakes: Assigning to a prop (text = ...) instead of using a default or a local derived value.
Expecting a prop change inside a child to flow back up to the parent.
Confusing 'I need a fallback' with 'I need to mutate the prop'.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Provide the fallback the React way: use a default prop value (or a derived constant) instead of reassigning the prop.

theory.question: What is the difference between props and state?
theory.directAnswer: Props are read-only inputs passed into a component from its parent; the component cannot change them. State is data a component owns and can update over time. Data flows down via props, and a child requests changes by calling a callback prop so the parent updates its state.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Props are the external configuration of a component (like function arguments). State is the internal, mutable memory of a component.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Separating immutable inputs (props) from mutable internal data (state) keeps data flow one-directional and predictable, which makes React apps easier to reason about and debug.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A parent renders a child with props. If the child needs to influence shared data, it calls a function the parent passed as a prop; the parent updates its own state and re-renders, sending new props down.

theory.whyImportant: This is the single most common React fundamentals question. Mixing up props and state leads to broken data flow and is a red flag in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: A Checkbox receives `checked` and `onChange` as props; the parent holds the actual boolean in state and updates it when onChange fires.

nestedTopics.title: One-way data flow
nestedTopics.explanation: Data moves from parent to child via props. Children never write to props; they signal upward via callbacks.

nestedTopics.title: Read-only props
nestedTopics.explanation: Mutating props is forbidden because the parent owns the value; React assumes props are stable inputs for a given render.

nestedTopics.title: Lifting state up
nestedTopics.explanation: When two siblings need the same data, you move the state to their common parent and pass it down as props.

followUps.question: Can a component change its own props?
followUps.answer: No. Props are read-only. To change what a child displays, the parent must re-render it with new prop values.

followUps.question: If a value never changes, should it be props or state?
followUps.answer: Props — or just a constant. State is only for values that change over the component's lifetime and should trigger re-renders.

scenario.question: A piece of data needs to reach a deeply nested component, so it's being passed through five intermediate components that don't use it. What is this called and how would you address it?
scenario.directAnswer: This is prop drilling — passing props through layers that only forward them. For small cases it's acceptable, but if it becomes painful you address it with composition (passing JSX as children so intermediates don't see the data) or by introducing React Context to provide the value directly where it's consumed.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Prop drilling is threading a prop down through many intermediate components that don't actually use it, just to reach a distant descendant.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It happens naturally because React's data flow is strictly one-way; the only built-in way to get data to a child is through its parents' props.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each intermediate component declares the prop and passes it along. Composition or Context lets you skip those intermediates entirely.

scenario.whyImportant: Recognizing prop drilling and knowing the trade-offs of fixing it (Context vs composition vs a store) shows you can reason about real component architecture.

nestedTopics.title: Composition as a fix
nestedTopics.explanation: Passing rendered JSX via children lets a parent supply content without intermediate components knowing about it.

nestedTopics.title: When drilling is fine
nestedTopics.explanation: One or two levels of explicit props is often clearer than introducing Context; don't over-engineer.

followUps.question: Does Context replace props entirely?
followUps.answer: No. Context is for cross-cutting values shared by many components; ordinary parent-child configuration should still use props.

coding.question: Build a reusable Button component that accepts a label and an onClick handler as props, with a disabled prop defaulting to false.
coding.thoughtProcess: A presentational Button should be configured entirely by props. I destructure label, onClick, and disabled (with a default), and forward them onto a native <button>. The component itself holds no state — all behavior comes from props passed by the parent.
coding.lineByLine: Button destructures label, onClick, and disabled with a default of false. It returns a native <button> wired to those props. App renders two Buttons with different props — proving the same component is reused with different configuration, and that <Button ... disabled /> passes disabled={true} via shorthand.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — rendering a single button is constant work.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — no additional data structures beyond the element itself.

alternativeApproaches.title: Spread the rest of the props
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use function Button({ label, ...rest }) and spread {...rest} onto the <button> so callers can pass any native attribute (type, aria-label) without you enumerating each one.

followUps.question: Why does <Button disabled /> work without ={true}?
followUps.answer: JSX treats a bare boolean attribute as true, so disabled is equivalent to disabled={true}.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Favor small, single-responsibility components configured by clear props. Separate presentational components (driven entirely by props) from container components (which own state and pass data down). Build a shared component library so teams compose pages from consistent primitives.
productionDeepDive.performance: Avoid creating new object, array, or inline-function props on every render when passing to memoized children — it defeats React.memo and triggers needless re-renders. Keep prop shapes stable and component trees shallow where reasonable.
productionDeepDive.security: Treat props that originate from user input as untrusted. Never pass unsanitized HTML into dangerouslySetInnerHTML through a prop. Validate and escape data before it flows into components that render it raw.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As the app grows, deeply drilled props become a maintenance burden. Introduce composition (children/slots) and, where truly cross-cutting, Context. Document component prop contracts (PropTypes or TypeScript) so large teams can use components safely.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer explicit, well-named props over a single opaque config object. Use TypeScript or PropTypes to make the prop contract self-documenting, and keep children for content rather than overloading props with JSX.
productionDeepDive.observability: React DevTools shows the component tree and the exact props each component received, making it easy to trace where a value came from and spot props that change unexpectedly between renders.

caseStudies.problem: Dozens of slightly different buttons existed across the app, causing visual drift and bugs.
caseStudies.solution: Built one Button component configured by props (variant, size, disabled) and replaced the ad-hoc copies.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: An upfront investment in a shared component vs long-term consistency and far less duplicated markup.
caseStudies.lessons: A small set of well-propped, reusable components beats many near-duplicate ones for both consistency and maintenance.

projectBuilder.summary: Build the presentational layer of the dashboard as reusable, prop-driven components: a StatCard, a UserRow, and a layout Panel that uses children.
requirements: A StatCard component that takes label and value props
A UserRow component that takes a user object as a prop and renders its fields
A Panel layout component that wraps arbitrary content via children
projectBuilder.architecture: Define purely presentational components that receive everything through props and hold no state. The dashboard page maps over data and renders these components, passing one item per component. Use children for layout containers like Panel.
projectBuilder.folderStructure:
src/
  components/
    StatCard.jsx
    UserRow.jsx
    Panel.jsx
  pages/
    Dashboard.jsx

steps.title: Create StatCard
steps.instructions: Build StatCard({ label, value }) that renders the label above the value. Render three of them from the dashboard with different props.
steps.checkpoint: Three stat cards display distinct labels and values.

steps.title: Create UserRow
steps.instructions: Build UserRow({ user }) that destructures user.name and user.email. Map an array of users to <UserRow> elements with a key.
steps.checkpoint: A list of users renders, one row per user.

steps.title: Create the Panel layout
steps.instructions: Build Panel({ title, children }) that renders a titled container and shows whatever is nested inside. Wrap the stats and the user list in Panels.
steps.checkpoint: Both sections sit inside titled panels using composition.

enhancements: Add a default prop for StatCard's value (e.g. '—')
Extract a Badge component and reuse it inside UserRow
interviewQuestions: Why are these components a good fit for being purely prop-driven and stateless?
How does the children prop let Panel stay reusable without knowing its content?

keyTakeaways: A component is a function that takes props and returns JSX; apps are trees of components.
Props are read-only inputs passed from parent to child — never mutate them.
Data flows one way (down); children request changes by calling callback props.
Destructure props for readability and use defaults for optional values.
Use the children prop for composition, and watch for prop drilling as trees get deep.
